items.title: Diving Into Data: Stories of Data-Inspired Journeys and Destinations
items.summary: What stories can data tell us—and what can we learn from the process of uncovering them? In this month’s episode of the Harvard Data Science Review Podcast, we speak with statistician Radu V. Craiu, the new editor of HDSR ’s Diving Into Data column, about the power of data to reveal surprising insights and the challenges of turning complex analyses into meaningful discoveries. Drawing on his research in statistical methodology and collaborations across fields such as genetics, astronomy, and demography, Craiu explores the importance of asking the right questions, recognizing the limitations of data, and learning from both successful analyses and those that don't go as planned. He also reflects on how artificial intelligence is reshaping the role of statisticians and why human judgment and statistical inference remain essential. The conversation also introduces Craiu’s vision for Diving Into Data , a column dedicated to making the often-hidden stories behind data science more accessible. In his call for submissions , published in HDSR’ s Fall 2026 issue (8.4), Craiu invites researchers and practitioners to share the discoveries, challenges, decisions, and even failures that shape their work with data, offering readers a glimpse into the process of data science. Our guest: Radu V. Craiu is a professor of statistical sciences at the University of Toronto and the editor of HDSR ’s Diving Into Data column. His research interests span computational methods in statistics, especially, Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms (MCMC), Bayesian inference, copula models, model selection procedures, and statistical genetics.

What stories can data tell us—and what can we learn from the process of uncovering them? In this month’s episode of the Harvard Data Science Review Podcast, we speak with statistician Radu V. Craiu, the new editor of HDSR’s Diving Into Data column, about the power of data to reveal surprising insights and the challenges of turning complex analyses into meaningful discoveries.

Drawing on his research in statistical methodology and collaborations across fields such as genetics, astronomy, and demography, Craiu explores the importance of asking the right questions, recognizing the limitations of data, and learning from both successful analyses and those that don't go as planned. He also reflects on how artificial intelligence is reshaping the role of statisticians and why human judgment and statistical inference remain essential.

The conversation also introduces Craiu’s vision for Diving Into Data, a column dedicated to making the often-hidden stories behind data science more accessible. In his call for submissions, published in HDSR’s Fall 2026 issue (8.4), Craiu invites researchers and practitioners to share the discoveries, challenges, decisions, and even failures that shape their work with data, offering readers a glimpse into the process of data science.

Our guest:

  • Radu V. Craiu is a professor of statistical sciences at the University of Toronto and the editor of HDSR’s Diving Into Data column. His research interests span computational methods in statistics, especially, Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms (MCMC), Bayesian inference, copula models, model selection procedures, and statistical genetics.

items.title: AI Agents Will Take 50% of Your Traffic — Is Your Data Ready? | Jeff Lunsford, CEO of Tealium
items.summary: 20% of enterprise website traffic is already coming from AI agents rather than humans, and that traffic converts at 38% more revenue per session than human visits. Within a year, Jeff Lunsford expects that number to reach 50%. Jeff, CEO of Tealium, joins Craig Smith to explain what this shift actually means for every business with a digital presence, and why the companies that will win are the ones whose data layer speaks fluently to agents, not just human browsers. Tealium operates as a neutral, real-time collection and distribution layer that sits underneath all of a company's customer-facing systems, capturing every interaction as it happens and distributing enriched identity-resolved profiles to whichever downstream system needs them - from personalization engines to fraud models - without storing the data itself. The most important argument Lunsford makes is one that Craig sets up precisely: agents need current state, consented context on demand, and a data warehouse offering yesterday's picture doesn't just underperform, it actively produces bad recommendations that erode trust in the AI system. He uses the pilot analogy he's carried for fifteen years: you don't want to fly knowing your altitude from yesterday, and for the same reason you don't want your customer-facing agent making decisions on stale data. The episode also covers the pattern that governs every channel transition in business history, brick-and-mortar didn't disappear when phones arrived, the internet didn't disappear when mobile arrived, and human website traffic won't disappear when agents arrive. Total session volume goes up because agents make it easier to initiate interactions. The businesses that prepared for each transition early captured disproportionate value. The businesses preparing their data layer for agentic consumption now are doing the same thing. Subscribe to Eye on A.I. for weekly conversations with the people building and deploying the future of AI.

20% of enterprise website traffic is already coming from AI agents rather than humans, and that traffic converts at 38% more revenue per session than human visits. Within a year, Jeff Lunsford expects that number to reach 50%. Jeff, CEO of Tealium, joins Craig Smith to explain what this shift actually means for every business with a digital presence, and why the companies that will win are the ones whose data layer speaks fluently to agents, not just human browsers. Tealium operates as a neutral, real-time collection and distribution layer that sits underneath all of a company's customer-facing systems, capturing every interaction as it happens and distributing enriched identity-resolved profiles to whichever downstream system needs them - from personalization engines to fraud models - without storing the data itself.

The most important argument Lunsford makes is one that Craig sets up precisely: agents need current state, consented context on demand, and a data warehouse offering yesterday's picture doesn't just underperform, it actively produces bad recommendations that erode trust in the AI system. He uses the pilot analogy he's carried for fifteen years: you don't want to fly knowing your altitude from yesterday, and for the same reason you don't want your customer-facing agent making decisions on stale data. The episode also covers the pattern that governs every channel transition in business history, brick-and-mortar didn't disappear when phones arrived, the internet didn't disappear when mobile arrived, and human website traffic won't disappear when agents arrive. Total session volume goes up because agents make it easier to initiate interactions. The businesses that prepared for each transition early captured disproportionate value. The businesses preparing their data layer for agentic consumption now are doing the same thing.
